video.title: The Most Hands-Off $192K/M Business Anyone Can Copy

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Lou van der Vier, a former HR worker and SEO agency owner who fires his agency clients and builds local lead-generation websites (geography plus service, e.g. towing, carpet cleaning, concrete), which he rents to local contractors for a flat monthly fee. He claims 232 sites and $192.5K in a month, with a mostly VA-run operation and 2-3 hours a week. He walks through his niche-selection process live, and describes moving to revenue share, phantom equity (profit interest) deals, and buying a catering business with an SBA loan for tax reasons. Key takeaway: owning the ranking asset and renting the leads is more passive than agency work, but it all rests on Lou's own unverified claims, and Chris is also selling a done-for-you version of the service.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; also promotes a done-for-you lead gen site service.

speakers.name: Lou van der Vier
speakers.description: Rents lead-generation websites to local businesses; ex-HR worker, ex-SEO agency owner; also does revenue-share deals and business acquisitions.

ideas.name: Rank-and-rent local lead-gen websites
ideas.one_liner: Build exact-match geography+service SEO sites in low-competition local niches, rank them in Google organic and Maps, and rent the resulting calls/leads to a local business for a flat monthly fee.
ideas.business_model: Flat monthly rental of lead flow to one local contractor per site (billed by card on file); sometimes converted to revenue share.
ideas.customer: Owner-operated local service businesses (towing, tree service, pest control, carpet cleaning, concrete, landscaping design, HVAC, etc.) that already spend on ads and have a decision-maker reachable by phone.
ideas.problem: Small local businesses get inconsistent leads, have been burned by marketing agencies, and don't know how to rank in Google.
ideas.offer: Calls and quote requests routed to the business from a site ranking at the top of organic results and Maps, with call tracking, for a flat monthly fee.

pricing.model: Flat monthly fee per site, roughly based on lead volume and ticket size

price_points.label: Bigger flat-fee clients before moving to rev share
Range from weak to well-optimised sites per Lou

pricing.notes: Lou runs a few days of free leads to test a buyer, then charges a flat fee. Landscaping must generate about $8,000 jobs to be worth it. Dentists would be ideal but are hard to reach.

acquisition_channels.details: Customers for the rented leads come via Google organic and Maps rankings. Exact-match domains (geography+service.com), a thousand-plus words per page and a separate page per service, targeting keywords with 500+ searches. Small cities of 60K-400K, 'low competition'. Sites can rank without links.

quote.text: I have a thousand words on the item every time, for all services.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

acquisition_channels.details: Sets up Google Business profiles; the Woodside site was number one in Maps instantly because the name matched the keyword. Later GBPs are obtained via the contractor, which Chris calls a 'false competitor'. A GBP suspension tanked the towing site.

To find paying buyers, Lou (now a VA) phones owners already advertising on Google or Meta, offering leads for a cut. He says most reply 'yeah, cool'. Where the owner is behind a gatekeeper he sometimes walks in. Buyers are tested by secret-shopper calls.

quote.text: I'm literally just calling the person and saying, hey, I know you don't know me from Adam, but I've got customers that want this.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

ideas.delivery: Sites are built in WordPress (Weebly originally), content drafted with AI (probably Claude per Lou) by VAs and human edited. Calls are tracked in CallRail, rank reports are sent by a VA, and the leads route straight to the business owner. Lou checks a weekly rank report and call report; most sites are left alone. Buyer outreach is done by a VA.
unit_economics_claims: Over 90% net profit margin (Chris's figure), 2-3 hours/week
Carpet cleaning site rented at $500/month for years at about $10/month cost
Costs ~ $50K/year of VAs plus hosting, CallRail and rank tracking
ideas.startup_cost: not stated (domain plus cheap shared hosting; Lou says site cost is about $10 a month or less)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About 2-3 months for the first six sites to rank, then rent them out; the first site took about 2.5 months to rank organically.

acquisition.how: The SEO and Maps side is inbound and can be agent-driven. Finding and pitching buyers needs phone calls, vetting and secret-shopping; this needs a human or VA. In the UK, cold outreach to sole traders is restricted by PECR/TPS.

onboarding.how: Short call to agree the deal, routing set-up, a few days of free trial, and manual vetting of buyers (checking they follow up the same day, answer professionally).

delivery.how: Agents can research niches, draft pages and FAQs, and monitor rankings and calls; VAs now do these. Link building and GBP creation still need people.

billing.how: Stripe card on file with auto-pay, no invoicing.

support.how: Mostly passive; handled via monitoring of ranks and call volume plus the occasional buyer conversation or replacement.

uk_applicability.notes: Local SEO and renting leads work the same in the UK, but the examples are US cities. UK constraints: PECR/TPS on cold calling sole traders, Google's rules on fake or virtual Business Profiles, the need to disclose ranking of lead-gen brands, and smaller local markets. Buyers like Checkatrade or MyBuilder compete for the same job.

risks: Google Business Profile suspension can tank a site (happened with Woodside towing)
Niches with long contracts (elevators) or middlemen (jets) don't rent out
Finding serious buyers is hard; some prideful owners won't pay even with obvious ROI
Buyer may stop following up leads or lie about closes
Rankings can be lost to competitors or algorithm changes
Fake or duplicate Business Profiles may breach Google policy

ideas.name: Revenue-share lead generation deals
ideas.one_liner: Convert the best rented sites from a flat fee to a ~20% revenue share and bring in friends' agencies to run ads for a cut of the cut.
ideas.business_model: Percentage of the contractor's gross (or net) revenue from leads.
ideas.customer: Existing high-paying rental clients with whom Lou has a trusting relationship.
ideas.problem: Flat fees cap earnings at around $4-5K a month even when a site generates much more value for the business.
ideas.offer: More leads in exchange for a share of revenue; Lou can add paid ads via partners to scale.

price_points.label: Typical rev share (20%, bumped to 25% if a partner agency is added)

pricing.notes: Gross vs net depends on niche (e.g. landscaping uses net due to materials). Lou claims 30-40K could replace 4-5K flat on a site.

acquisition_channels.details: He pitched his largest existing flat-fee clients, e.g. the $5K/month ones; idea came from another guest, Bradley.

quote.text: I reached out to my highest paying clients, like the bigger flat fees for five grand a month clients.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

ideas.delivery: Same sites plus extra GBPs, ads run by partner agencies. Lou audits via read access to the client's CRM and payment system, and phones their customers pretending to run a satisfaction survey.
unit_economics_claims: Lou says revenue share drove a 'straight ramp' in income
Takes 20% of gross; $30-40K versus $4-5K flat for a site

acquisition.how: Needs trust-based conversations with existing clients.

onboarding.how: Negotiating terms and getting CRM and payment read access is manual.

delivery.how: Lead generation and rank monitoring as I1; ads management delegated to partners.

billing.how: Needs verifying the client's revenue figures and calculating share, so is not hands-off.

uk_applicability.notes: Rev-share contracts are legal in the UK; just document clearly and protect data under UK GDPR when accessing client CRMs.

risks: Business owner may under-report closes or margins
Needs high trust and an existing relationship
Percentage of gross can be disputed in material-heavy trades

quotes.text: I'm asking for a read access to their CRM and their payment system.
quotes.speaker: Lou van der Vier

ideas.name: Profit interest (phantom equity) for SEO
ideas.one_liner: Take a share of a business's future sale price in exchange for lead generation, on top of a revenue share.
ideas.business_model: Revenue share now plus a percentage of the company's exit value.
ideas.customer: Established local companies with a trusted relationship (e.g. a paving company valued at $3.5M).
ideas.problem: Business owners want growth, and Lou wants long-term upside rather than only monthly fees.
ideas.offer: SEO-driven growth in exchange for revenue share and ~20% of the company on sale.

acquisition_channels.details: Arose from a good rapport with an existing paving client, not scalable.

ideas.delivery: Lou pushes the company's SEO and leads as hard as possible.

delivery.how: SEO and lead generation as in I1.

uk_applicability.notes: Needs UK legal advice (growth shares, EMI, or contractual profit share); US-style 'profit interest' is an LLC concept.

risks: Depends on the owner's honesty and a sale happening

quotes.text: I just got a paving deal for that. Their companies were three and a half million and I just got 20% of it.
quotes.speaker: Lou van der Vier

ideas.name: Buying a small business with an SBA loan and growing it via SEO
ideas.one_liner: Buy an existing baby-boomer-owned business (a catering company), install a family operator, and feed it leads through SEO, partly for tax reasons.
ideas.business_model: Owner of an operating business; the profit comes from running the business with leads from SEO.
ideas.problem: Lou had large taxes on rental income and wanted an asset that offsets them and grows with his lead gen skills.
ideas.offer: Existing catering company bought for $1.7M with an operator, plus lead generation.

acquisition_channels.details: Uses SEO and lead generation to grow the acquired business.

ideas.delivery: Lou's brother, previously a car wash operations manager, runs it for half the company.

acquisition.how: SEO and ads can supply leads.

delivery.how: Food preparation and events are physical work.

uk_applicability.notes: SBA loans and the US tax treatment (asset depreciation offsets) don't exist in the UK; UK equivalents differ (e.g. Start Up Loans, capital allowances).

risks: Lack of experience in the industry
Tax advice is hearsay from his CPA

tactics.name: Niche and city screening on Google Maps and organic
steps: Pick a trade from Thumbtack's near-me categories, favouring home improvement and high-ticket jobs
Search the trade plus a mid-sized city, skipping sponsored ads
In the Maps pack look for under 10 reviews, no website or only a social profile, and no exact-match business names
In organic results look for inner pages, directories, Yelp and thin content (e.g. ~400 words)
Compare keyword variants with Google Trends to avoid false positives
Skip the niche if competitors have dozens or hundreds of reviews

quote.text: I want to see really low. So like less than 10 reviews.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

tactics.name: Content blueprint beating competitors
steps: Review competitor sites in the niche and also in top competitive cities
List topics, then check keyword volumes (about 500+ searches get their own page)
Build a home page, about, contact and separate service pages for every service
Write about 1,000 words per topic, including commercial and transactional keywords
Use ChatGPT to find common customer questions from Yelp and Reddit and add an FAQ
Add both a click-to-call button and a quote form
Use a human edit over AI-drafted copy

quote.text: I'll go look out at all the competitors in that niche.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

tactics.name: Vetting a lead buyer
steps: Target local owners already paying for ads (check Meta Ad Library and Google)
Avoid national call centres
Give leads for free for a few days
Ask how quickly they follow up; drop those who don't call back the same day
Secret-shop their phone answering
Call their customers pretending to run a satisfaction survey to check closes and prices
Start with commission, then switch to a flat fee once they close

quote.text: if they tell me today, and they don't call today, they're done.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

tactics.name: Rev share with partner agencies
steps: Pitch top flat-fee clients on revenue share
Request read access to their CRM and payments
Bring in friends' agencies to run Facebook/Google ads and split Lou's cut
Ask the owner to bump 20% to 25% to cover partners

tactics.name: Weekly monitoring dashboard
steps: A VA sends a Monday rank report and a call tracking report
Investigate only if both rankings and call volume fall
Use historical data to identify seasonality
Stripe card on file with auto-pay for billing

tactics.name: Getting Google Business Profiles via the contractor
steps: Rank organically first and prove lead flow
Once the contractor is paying, ask him to help create additional profiles

quote.text: I generally work with the contractor.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

warnings.warning: Shiny object syndrome: pick niches rigorously and follow one process.

warnings.warning: Link building is the hard part; follow one teacher rather than mixing sources.

quote.text: Follow one person instead of multiple.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

warnings.warning: Rev share requires strong trust; do not offer it to brand-new customers.
Don't give leads away free for long.

lessons.lesson: Owning the asset beats renting out your skill: Lou swapped client-controlled agency work for owned sites that he rents out.

quote.text: if I own the asset 'cause then he can't tell me what to do
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

lessons.lesson: Vertical integration: use a skill you already sell (SEO) to build your own revenue-producing assets.
Solving an everyday annoyance (a wrecked car and a tow company with no idea where its leads come from) can reveal real demand.
Pick less competitive markets where decision-makers answer the phone and tickets are high; there are millions of service+geography combinations.
Free has no value; test buyers briefly, then charge, and vet them with secret-shopper checks.

quote.text: I believe free has no value.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

lessons.lesson: Finding the right buyer is harder than generating leads; some owners refuse positive-ROI deals out of pride.

quote.text: I think it's finding a buyer, finding the right buyer.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

lessons.lesson: Moving from flat fee to revenue share on the biggest clients can multiply income without taking on more clients.
Delegating content, outreach and reporting to VAs keeps the founder to a couple of hours per week.
Burning the boats (quitting all agency clients at once) forced focus but was risky.
AI makes content creation and research cheaper, and the host believes local services are among the last to be hit by AI search.
Organic rankings convert better and churn less than ads because searchers trust the top result.

quote.text: There's really not much churn.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest is a first-hand operator with specific process detail (niche screening, content, vetting buyers, costs), but headline numbers ($192.5K/month, 232 sites, 90% margin) are self-reported and unverified, and the transcript is low-quality Whisper-tiny with some mis-heard words. The guest sells coaching and the host promotes a done-for-you service.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Lou promotes his coaching (websiterentalcoaching.com as heard) and Chris promotes a 'Done for You' lead-gen site build service and a Beehiiv sponsor read.
